Their pups are born with dark fur that turns white as they grow.
text.size_comparison.young: On all fours, they reach your shoulders — around 2 feet 7 inches at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a big suitcase — around 99 pounds.
text.map_narration: Arctic wolves live in the frozen tundra of northern Canada and Greenland.
text.sound_description.young: Arctic Wolves howl long and loud to talk to their pack across the frozen wilderness.

text.summary.young: Snow leopards are big cats that live high in the mountains of Asia. Their tail is almost as long as their body and wraps around them like a scarf to keep warm in the freezing cold.
text.summary.tiny: Snow leopards live where mountains touch the sky and the air is freezing cold. Their fluffy tail wraps around them like a scarf.
fun_facts.young: A snow leopard's tail is nearly as long as its whole body!
They can survive in freezing temperatures as cold as -40 degrees.
Snow leopards have such powerful legs they can pounce on prey from 50 feet away.
Their spotted coat helps them blend into rocky mountain slopes perfectly.
They wrap their fluffy tail around their face like a warm blanket when they sleep.
They live higher up in the mountains than almost any other big cat.
fun_facts.tiny: Their tail is almost as long as their whole body.
They can leap over a school bus in one giant jump.
Their huge paws work like snowshoes so they don't sink in the snow.
did_you_know.young: They can jump six times their body length — that's like jumping over a school bus!
Their huge paws work like snowshoes to help them walk on deep snow without sinking.
They can't roar like other big cats — they make a soft chuffing sound instead.
Their thick fur can have up to 26,000 hairs in one tiny spot the size of your fingernail!
They hunt at dawn and dusk when other animals are resting.
text.size_comparison.young: On all fours, they reach your chest — around 2 feet 4 inches at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a big suitcase — around 99 pounds.
text.map_narration: Snow leopards live high in the mountains of Central Asia, including the Himalayas.
text.sound_description.young: They make a soft chuffing sound by puffing air through their nose and mouth — they can't roar like lions.

text.summary.young: Camels are large desert animals with humps on their backs, found in Asia and Africa. Their humps store fat — not water — which they turn into energy so they can go over a week without drinking.
text.summary.tiny: Camels have humps on their backs that store fat — not water! They can go more than a week without drinking.
fun_facts.young: Camels spit when they're annoyed — it's actually their stomach contents!
Baby camels are born without humps.
They can eat thorny plants that would hurt other animals' mouths.
They've been helping people cross deserts for over 4,000 years.
A thirsty camel can smell water from miles away.
They can close their nostrils completely to keep out blowing sand.
fun_facts.tiny: Baby camels are born without humps.
They can close their nostrils to keep sand out.
They can smell water from really far away.
did_you_know.young: They can drink 40 gallons of water in one go — that's enough to fill a bathtub!
Their thick eyelashes and closeable nostrils keep sand out during desert storms.
They can survive losing 25% of their body weight in water — humans would be in danger at just 15%.
Their wide, flat feet work like snowshoes on sand, so they don't sink in.
A camel's body temperature can change by 11 degrees to avoid sweating and save water.
text.size_comparison.young: Way taller than any grown-up — their hump reaches about 7 feet high!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a horse — around 1,300 pounds.
text.map_narration: Camels live in the deserts of the Middle East, Central Asia, and North Africa.
text.sound_description.young: They make deep grunting and groaning sounds, and sometimes loud bellows when they're upset.

fennec_fox.name: Fennec Fox
fennec_fox.habitat: Sandy deserts in North Africa and the Middle East

text.summary.young: Fennec foxes are tiny foxes with huge ears that live in the deserts of North Africa and the Middle East. Their giant ears work like air conditioners to keep them cool and can hear insects crawling underground from far away.
text.summary.tiny: Fennec foxes have the biggest ears of any fox — ears so huge they can hear a beetle walking under the sand! They're the tiniest foxes in the world and live in sandy deserts where it's boiling hot.
fun_facts.young: Fennec foxes dig underground burrows to escape the blazing desert heat during the day.
Baby fennec foxes are called kits and their eyes stay closed for the first two weeks of life.
These tiny foxes can jump up to 60 centimetres high and 120 centimetres forward in one leap!
They eat insects, lizards, birds, eggs, and even desert plants.
Their cream-coloured fur helps them blend into the sandy desert so predators can't spot them easily.
They are most active at night when the desert cools down and it's easier to hunt.
fun_facts.tiny: They can leap as high as your kitchen table in one jump!
Their furry feet work like slippers on hot sand so they don't burn their paws.
Baby fennecs keep their eyes closed for two whole weeks after they're born.
did_you_know.young: A fennec fox's ears can be 15 centimetres long — that's half as long as their whole body!
They can go for a long time without drinking water because they get moisture from their food.
Their thick, fluffy fur keeps them warm during cold desert nights and cool during hot days.
They have furry feet that work like snowshoes to help them walk on hot sand without burning their paws.
They are the smallest fox species in the world — they only weigh as much as a small bag of sugar!
text.size_comparison.young: The smallest fox in the world — they barely reach your knees, around 8 inches at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a carton of milk — around 3 pounds.
text.map_narration: Fennec foxes live in the sandy deserts of North Africa and the Sahara.
text.sound_description.young: They make high-pitched barks, chirps, purrs, and growls to talk to each other.

text.summary.young: Kangaroos are large hopping animals that live in Australia. They can't walk backwards because their powerful legs and big tail only work for moving forward.
text.summary.tiny: Kangaroos are hopping animals with powerful legs and a big bouncy tail. They can't walk backwards — only forwards!
fun_facts.young: Kangaroos are the only large animals that hop to get around
A group of kangaroos is called a mob
They can't sweat so they lick their arms to cool down on hot days
Male kangaroos flex their muscles and fight by boxing to impress females
They use less energy hopping fast than hopping slowly because they bounce like a spring
Newborn joeys climb into their mother's pouch and stay there for months growing bigger
fun_facts.tiny: They are the only big animals that hop everywhere they go.
Baby kangaroos are as tiny as jellybeans when they're born.
They lick their arms to cool down when it's hot.
did_you_know.young: A baby kangaroo is called a joey and is only as big as a jellybean when it's born
They can hop as fast as a car on a road — up to 56 kilometres per hour
A kangaroo's tail is so strong it acts like a fifth leg when they walk slowly
They can jump over three cars lined up in a row — that's 9 metres in one leap
Mother kangaroos can pause their pregnancy if food is scarce and wait until conditions are better
text.size_comparison.young: Standing tall on their hind legs, they are taller than most grown-ups — around 5 feet 3 inches!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a grown-up — around 154 pounds.
text.map_narration: Kangaroos live in the grasslands, forests, and deserts of Australia.
text.sound_description.young: They make thumping sounds with their feet to warn others of danger and grunt or hiss when they're upset.

red_kangaroo.name: Red Kangaroo
red_kangaroo.habitat: Dry grasslands and deserts of Australia

text.summary.young: Red kangaroos are the largest marsupials in the world and live in the dry grasslands of Australia. They can hop as fast as a car on a city street — up to 60 kilometres per hour — and the faster they hop, the less tired they get!
text.summary.tiny: Red kangaroos hop faster than a car driving through town. The faster they hop, the less tired they get!
fun_facts.young: Red kangaroos use their strong tail like an extra leg when they walk slowly.
They can hop faster than most people can run on a bicycle!
Joeys stay safe inside their mother's pouch for about 6 months before peeking out.
They cool down by licking their arms when it's hot outside.
They live in groups called mobs — sometimes with 10 or more kangaroos together.
Their powerful back legs can kick hard enough to protect them from dingoes and other predators.
fun_facts.tiny: They use their strong tail like an extra leg when they walk.
Baby kangaroos are called joeys and they're tiny as jellybeans when they're born.
They lick their arms to cool down when it's hot.
did_you_know.young: They can jump 8 metres in one hop — that's longer than a school bus is wide!
Baby kangaroos are called joeys and are tiny when born — about the size of a jellybean!
They can't walk backwards — their big tail and strong back legs won't let them.
They can survive without drinking water for months by getting moisture from the plants they eat.
Male red kangaroos are bright red, but females are blue-grey — so they're sometimes called blue fliers!
text.size_comparison.young: The biggest kangaroo — standing up, they are taller than a grown-up, around 5 feet 11 inches!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a grown-up and a bit more — around 200 pounds.
text.map_narration: Red kangaroos live in the dry grasslands and deserts of central Australia.
text.sound_description.young: They make soft grunting and clicking sounds to talk to each other, and hiss when they feel threatened.

text.summary.young: The platypus is a special mammal that lives in rivers and streams in Australia. It's one of only five mammals in the world that lays eggs instead of having babies!
text.summary.tiny: The platypus is one of the most unusual animals on Earth — it lays eggs like a bird but feeds milk to its babies. It lives in rivers in Australia and has a duck's bill, a beaver's tail, and webbed feet.
fun_facts.young: The platypus has a bill like a duck, a tail like a beaver, and webbed feet like an otter.
Platypuses don't have teeth — they scoop up mud and use gravel to grind up their food.
A platypus can hold its breath underwater for up to two minutes while hunting.
They use special sensors in their bills to detect tiny electric signals from hiding prey.
When scientists first saw a platypus in 1798, they thought someone had sewn different animals together as a joke!
They make burrows in riverbanks that can be as long as a school bus.
fun_facts.tiny: A platypus can stay underwater for two whole minutes while it hunts for food.
It closes its eyes and ears when it dives, so it finds food by feeling tiny electric tingles through its bill.
When people first saw a platypus, they thought someone had stuck different animals together as a trick!
did_you_know.young: Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their back legs that can hurt other animals.
They close their eyes and ears when they dive underwater to hunt.
A platypus can eat half its body weight in food every single day!
Baby platypuses are called puggles and are only the size of a jellybean when they hatch.
They glow blue-green under special UV light — scientists only discovered this in 2020!
text.size_comparison.young: About as long as a school ruler and a half — with a duck bill, beaver tail, and otter feet!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a carton of milk — around 3 pounds.
text.map_narration: Platypuses live along the rivers and streams of eastern Australia and Tasmania.
text.sound_description.young: They make soft chirping and growling sounds when they're on land.

tasmanian_devil.name: Tasmanian Devil
tasmanian_devil.habitat: Forests and coastal areas of Tasmania

text.summary.young: Tasmanian Devils are small black marsupials that live only on the island of Tasmania in Australia. They have the strongest bite for their size of any mammal alive today — strong enough to crunch through bones!
text.summary.tiny: Tasmanian Devils are black night animals with the strongest bite for their size in the whole world. They can crunch right through bones!
fun_facts.young: Tasmanian Devils eat almost everything — bones, fur, and even teeth!
They make loud screaming and growling sounds when they eat together.
Baby Tasmanian Devils are about the size of a grain of rice when they're born.
They have whiskers on their face and body that help them find food in the dark.
They store extra fat in their tail when food is plentiful.
They are the largest carnivorous marsupial in the world.
fun_facts.tiny: They eat everything — bones, fur, even teeth.
Baby Tasmanian Devils are tiny as a rice grain when they're born.
Their tail gets fat and round when there's lots of food around.
did_you_know.young: They can eat up to 40% of their body weight in just 30 minutes.
They got their name because early settlers heard their scary screams at night.
They are marsupials, which means babies grow in their mother's pouch.
When they feel threatened, their ears turn bright red.
They can climb trees and swim across rivers.
text.size_comparison.young: Small but fierce — right at your knees, around 1 foot at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a bowling ball — around 18 pounds.
text.map_narration: Tasmanian devils live only on the island of Tasmania, south of Australia.
text.sound_description.young: They screech, growl, and snarl loudly — especially when they're eating together.

panda.name: Panda
panda.habitat: Bamboo forests in the mountains of China

text.summary.young: Giant pandas are large black-and-white bears that live in the bamboo forests of China. They spend up to 16 hours every day eating bamboo because it gives them very little energy.
text.summary.tiny: Pandas are big black-and-white bears that munch bamboo all day long. They live in the mountain forests of China.
fun_facts.young: Giant pandas have lived on Earth for about 2 million years.
Pandas are excellent climbers and sometimes sleep in trees.
A panda's jaw muscles are so strong they can crush thick bamboo stems.
Giant pandas spend most of their time sitting down while they eat.
They can poop up to 40 times a day because bamboo is hard to digest.
In the wild, giant pandas are shy and usually live alone.
fun_facts.tiny: They spend most of their day sitting down, eating bamboo.
They're brilliant climbers and sometimes have naps up in the trees.
A panda can poop more than forty times every single day!
did_you_know.young: A giant panda can eat up to 40 pounds of bamboo in a single day.
Baby pandas are pink, hairless, and about the size of a stick of butter when they're born.
Giant pandas have a special thumb-like bone that helps them grip bamboo stalks.
They sometimes do somersaults and roll down hills just for fun.
A panda's black eye patches make each one look unique, like fingerprints.
text.size_comparison.young: On all fours, they reach your shoulders — around 2 feet 7 inches at the shoulder. When they sit up, they're almost as tall as you!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as two grown-ups — around 265 pounds.
text.map_narration: Giant pandas live in the misty bamboo forests of central China.
text.sound_description.young: Giant pandas make huffing and bleating sounds, and sometimes honk when they're playful or upset.

text.summary.young: Red pandas are small furry animals that live in the mountain forests of Asia. They use their long bushy tail as a blanket to stay warm in winter.
text.summary.tiny: Red pandas have ginger fur and a stripy tail as long as their whole body. They sleep curled up in trees with their tail wrapped round them like a cosy scarf.
fun_facts.young: Red pandas have a special wrist bone that works like a thumb to help them grip bamboo.
They sleep in trees during the day and wake up at dusk to look for food.
A red panda's reddish-brown fur helps them hide among the red moss and white lichen in their forest home.
They clean their fur like cats do — by licking their paws and rubbing their face.
They make squeaking and whistling sounds to talk to each other.
They walk a bit like raccoons and some people call them 'firefox.'
fun_facts.tiny: They have a special wrist bone that works a bit like your thumb to grip bamboo.
They walk down trees headfirst because their back ankles can twist right round.
They make little huffing sounds when they're happy.
did_you_know.young: They aren't closely related to giant pandas at all — they're in their own special animal family.
They spend most of their time in trees and are excellent climbers.
A red panda's thick fur coat keeps them warm in cold mountain weather.
They eat mostly bamboo, but they also munch on fruits, berries, and insects.
Baby red pandas are called cubs and stay with their mother for about a year.
text.size_comparison.young: Small and adorable, they only stand your knees — around 11 inches at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a house cat — around 11 pounds.
text.map_narration: Red pandas live in the cool mountain forests of Nepal, China, and Myanmar.
text.sound_description.young: They make squeaking, chirping, and whistling sounds to talk to each other.

ibex.name: Ibex
ibex.habitat: Rocky mountain cliffs and steep slopes

text.summary.young: Ibex are wild goats with huge curved horns that live high in rocky mountains across Europe, Asia, and Africa. They can climb straight up nearly vertical dam walls to lick salt and minerals from the stone — their split hooves grip like suction cups.
text.summary.tiny: Ibex are wild goats with huge curved horns that climb straight up rocky cliffs. They're so good at climbing they walk up dam walls to lick salty stones.
fun_facts.young: Ibex live higher up mountains than almost any other large animal — some live above 16,000 feet where the air is thin and cold.
Male ibex grow a long beard under their chin that gets darker and longer as they get older.
They eat grass, leaves, and twigs — and they love licking salty minerals from rocks.
In winter, ibex climb down to lower slopes where there's more food and less snow.
A male ibex can weigh as much as a baby grand piano!
Female ibex live in groups called herds, but adult males often wander alone.
fun_facts.tiny: Male ibex have long beards that get darker as they grow older.
Baby ibex can climb steep rocks just hours after they're born.
They jump as high as your bedroom ceiling from standing still.
did_you_know.young: An ibex's horns can grow over a meter long — that's taller than a 6-year-old!
They kids can climb rocky cliffs just hours after being born.
Male ibex fight by rearing up and smashing their horns together — the crash can be heard across a whole valley!
They can jump over 6 feet straight up in the air from a standing position.
An ibex's hooves have a hard outer edge and a soft rubbery center that grips rock like a climbing shoe.
text.size_comparison.young: On all fours, they reach your chin — around 2 feet 11 inches at the shoulder. Their long curved horns make them look even more impressive!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as two grown-ups — around 220 pounds.
text.map_narration: Ibex live high up in the mountains of Europe, Asia, and North Africa.
text.sound_description.young: They make bleating sounds like goats — a loud 'baa' to call to each other across mountain cliffs.

text.summary.young: Caribou are large deer that live in the cold forests and tundra of North America, Europe, and Asia. They are the only deer where both boys and girls grow antlers — and they travel farther than any other land animal, walking up to 5,000 kilometres every year!
text.summary.tiny: Caribou are the only deer where mums AND dads grow antlers! They walk farther than any other animal on land — all the way across snowy mountains and frozen rivers.
fun_facts.young: Caribou have special fur with hollow hairs that trap air to keep them warm in freezing cold weather.
Their noses warm up the icy air before it goes into their lungs.
They can smell food buried under a metre of snow!
They travel in huge herds — sometimes thousands of caribou walk together.
They shed their antlers every year and grow brand new ones.
In winter, caribou dig through snow with their hooves to find plants to eat.
fun_facts.tiny: Their fur is filled with tiny air bubbles that keep them toasty warm.
They can smell plants hiding under deep snow.
A baby caribou can stand up and walk before you've finished lunch!
did_you_know.young: They are the only deer where both males and females grow antlers.
They migrate up to 5,000 kilometres every year — the longest land migration of any animal on Earth!
Their wide hooves work like snowshoes to help them walk on deep snow without sinking.
They can swim really well and cross wide rivers during their long journeys.
A baby caribou can stand and walk just 90 minutes after being born.
text.size_comparison.young: Taller than you at the shoulder on all fours — about 3 feet 11 inches at the shoulder. Their big antlers make them look even taller!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as two grown-ups — around 331 pounds.
text.map_narration: Caribou roam the Arctic tundra and forests of North America, Europe, and Asia.
text.sound_description.young: They make grunting and snorting sounds to talk to each other in the herd.

text.summary.young: Walruses are large marine mammals that live in the icy Arctic Ocean. They use their long tusks like a cane to pull themselves out of the water onto ice.
text.summary.tiny: Walruses use their tusks like walking sticks to climb onto the ice. They turn pink when they're warm!
fun_facts.young: Walruses turn pink when they get warm because blood rushes to their skin
They have a special air sac in their throat that works like a built-in life jacket
They sleep in the water with their head bobbing above the surface
Their scientific name means 'tooth-walking sea horse'
They can slow down their heartbeat to save oxygen when diving
A group of walruses on land is called a haulout
fun_facts.tiny: They have a special pocket in their throat that puffs up like a balloon to help them float.
They sleep in the water with their heads bobbing up and down like apples.
A walrus can eat thousands of clams in one meal using its super-sensitive whiskers to find them in the dark.
did_you_know.young: A walrus's tusks never stop growing and can reach over 1 meter long
They can hold their breath underwater for up to 30 minutes
Their whiskers help them find clams buried in the dark ocean floor
They can eat over 6,000 clams in one meal
Baby walruses can swim as soon as they are born
text.size_comparison.young: About as long as a small car — around 10 feet, with giant tusks that can be 3 feet long!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a small car — around 2,600 pounds.
text.map_narration: Walruses live on the ice floes and coastlines of the Arctic Ocean.
text.sound_description.young: They grunt, bellow, and whistle to talk to each other.

text.summary.young: Musk oxen are shaggy Arctic animals with curved horns that live in the coldest parts of North America and Greenland. When wolves attack, they form a protective circle with their horns pointing out and their babies safe in the middle.
text.summary.tiny: Musk oxen are shaggy giants with curved horns who live where it's freezing cold all year. When danger comes, they stand in a circle with their babies tucked safely in the middle.
fun_facts.young: A musk ox's fur coat is so thick that snow doesn't melt when it lands on them.
Male musk oxen run at each other at 35 miles per hour and crash their heads together to see who's strongest.
Musk oxen have survived in the Arctic for thousands of years — even living alongside woolly mammoths during the Ice Age.
Their hooves have sharp edges that work like ice skates to grip slippery frozen ground.
Musk oxen only shed their soft undercoat once a year in summer, and people collect it to make the softest scarves in the world.
A group of musk oxen is called a herd, and they stay together all year long for warmth and protection.
fun_facts.tiny: Their fur is so thick that snow lands on them and doesn't even melt.
They've been alive since the Ice Age, living alongside woolly mammoths.
Their hooves have sharp edges that grip ice like tiny climbing boots.
did_you_know.young: Musk oxen have two layers of fur — a soft undercoat called qiviut that's eight times warmer than sheep's wool, and long guard hairs that can reach the ground.
Their curved horns meet in the middle of their head to form a thick helmet called a boss that protects their skull when they crash into each other.
Musk oxen can smell food buried under three feet of snow and use their strong hooves to dig through the ice.
Despite their name, musk oxen aren't oxen at all — they're more closely related to sheep and goats.
Baby musk oxen can run and keep up with the herd just hours after being born.
text.size_comparison.young: Massive and shaggy — about 4 feet 7 inches at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as five or six grown-ups — around 882 pounds.
text.map_narration: Musk oxen live in the frozen tundra of the Arctic, in Canada, Greenland, and Alaska.
text.sound_description.young: They make deep grunting and snorting sounds, and males bellow loudly during fights.

text.summary.young: Armadillos are small mammals with hard, bony shells that live in North and South America. Three-banded armadillos can roll into a perfect ball that clicks shut like a fortress — no predator can pry it open.
fun_facts.young: Armadillos can jump three to four feet straight up in the air when startled.
They use their strong claws to dig burrows up to 15 feet long.
They eat insects, grubs, worms, and sometimes fruit and plants.
Their name means 'little armored one' in Spanish.
Some armadillos can inflate their stomachs and intestines with air to help them float across water.
They sleep up to 16 hours a day in their underground burrows.
did_you_know.young: They are the only mammals with shells made of bone.
They can hold their breath for up to six minutes when digging.
Baby armadillos are born with soft, leathery shells that harden as they grow.
They can walk underwater along the bottom of rivers and streams.
They have poor eyesight but an amazing sense of smell to find food underground.
text.size_comparison.young: Only about as tall as a football, with a hard shell like a suit of armour — around 9 inches at the shoulder.
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a couple bags of sugar — around 13 pounds.
text.map_narration: Armadillos live in the grasslands and forests of the Americas, from the United States to Argentina.
text.sound_description.young: They make soft grunting and squeaking sounds, and snuffle noisily when they dig for food.

emu.name: Emu
emu.habitat: Open grasslands and forests across Australia

text.summary.young: Emus are giant birds that live in Australia and cannot fly. They have powerful legs that let them run as fast as a car drives through a neighborhood.
fun_facts.young: Emus are the second tallest birds in the world — only ostriches are taller.
Their feathers look like shaggy fur and help keep them cool in the hot Australian sun.
They love water and are excellent swimmers.
They can travel over 15 kilometers in a single day looking for food.
They chicks have stripes like tiny zebras to help them hide from predators.
An emu's kick is so strong it can break bones — they use their powerful legs to protect themselves.
did_you_know.young: They can run up to 50 kilometers per hour — that's faster than most people can ride a bike!
Male emus sit on the eggs for eight weeks without eating or drinking while the females leave to find more mates.
They have two sets of eyelids — one for blinking and one for keeping dust out of their eyes.
In 1932, Australian soldiers tried to reduce the emu population but the emus were too fast and too clever — the birds won!
They swallow stones to help grind up food in their stomachs because they don't have teeth.
text.size_comparison.young: The second tallest bird in the world — they stand about 6 feet tall, way taller than you!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a big suitcase — around 121 pounds.
text.map_narration: Emus live in the open grasslands, forests, and deserts of Australia.
text.sound_description.young: They make deep booming and drumming sounds that rumble like distant thunder.

text.summary.young: Lemurs are furry primates that only live on the island of Madagascar. Ring-tailed lemurs have stink fights — they rub scent on their tails and wave them at rivals to see who smells the strongest!
fun_facts.young: Ring-tailed lemurs spend more time on the ground than any other lemur.
Lemurs have a special claw just for grooming their fur!
Girl lemurs are the bosses — they eat first and lead the group.
They have wet noses like dogs to help them smell better.
Some lemurs can leap 25 feet between trees — that's longer than a school bus is wide!
They eat fruit, leaves, flowers, and even bugs.
did_you_know.young: They can only be found wild in Madagascar — nowhere else on Earth!
A ring-tailed lemur's tail has 13 black and white stripes.
They love to sunbathe! They sit with their arms out like they're soaking up the warmth.
Some lemurs sing together in groups — their calls sound like whale songs!
Baby lemurs cling to their mother's belly for the first few weeks of life.
text.size_comparison.young: Their body is about as long as a ruler — but their stripy tail is even longer!
text.weight_comparison.young: They weigh about as much as a bag of sugar — around 7 pounds.
text.map_narration: Lemurs live only on the island of Madagascar, off the coast of Africa.
text.sound_description.young: They make chirping and purring sounds to talk to their families, and loud calls to warn about danger.

text.summary.young: The Amur tiger is the biggest cat in the whole world, with thick orange fur and bold black stripes. It lives in the cold, snowy forests of far-off eastern Russia, padding silently through the trees. Every single tiger has its very own pattern of stripes, just like a fingerprint.
text.summary.tiny: The Amur tiger is the biggest cat in the world. It has bright orange fur with bold black stripes, and it lives where it's snowy and cold.
fun_facts.young: No two tigers have the same stripes — its pattern is all its own, just like a fingerprint.
Its thick, furry coat keeps it warm and cosy even when snow is falling all around.
It has soft, padded paws, so it can creep through the forest without making a sound.
When the Amur tiger leaps after its dinner, it can spring as far as a small car is long.
It loves the water and is a strong, happy swimmer, even in chilly rivers.
Its stripes are like hide-and-seek magic, helping it blend into the long grass and trees.
fun_facts.tiny: Every tiger has its very own stripes, like a special pattern.
Its thick fur keeps it warm and cosy in the snow.
It creeps through the forest so softly, not even the snow hears it.
did_you_know.young: In one big meal it can eat more than you would eat in many days.
A tiger's roar is so deep and loud that you could hear it from far across the forest.
Its long tail helps it balance and steer when it runs and turns quickly.
Even the skin under its striped fur has a stripey pattern.
There are very few of these tigers left in the wild, so they are carefully protected.
Tigers have their very own day — every July 29 is International Tiger Day, when people celebrate big cats and help keep them safe.
text.size_comparison.young: It's enormous — about ten feet long from its nose to the tip of its tail, which is longer than three children lying down in a row.
text.weight_comparison.young: It's very heavy — about four hundred and forty pounds, as much as two or three grown-ups standing on one scale together.
text.map_narration: Padding silently through cold, snowy forests, it lives in the far east of Russia.
text.sound_description.young: When it wants to warn other tigers to stay away, it lets out a deep, rumbling roar that booms through the trees. Up close and friendly, it makes a soft, puffing sound called a chuff.

text.summary.young: The pangolin is the only mammal in the world covered all over in scales — and they're made of the same stuff as your very own fingernails! When it feels scared, it tucks in tight and rolls itself into a perfect little ball. It slurps up ants and termites with a tongue that's longer than its whole body.
text.summary.tiny: The pangolin is covered in scales, like a tiny walking pinecone. When it gets scared, it rolls into a little ball!
fun_facts.young: Its scales are made of the same stuff as your fingernails, and they cover it like overlapping armour.
When something startles it, it rolls into a tight ball so only its hard scales show.
Its sticky tongue is longer than its whole body — perfect for slurping ants out of their nests.
It has no teeth at all, so it swallows tiny stones to help mash up its food inside.
It walks on its back legs sometimes, holding its front paws up like little hands.
The pangolin can close up its ears and nose to keep out angry, biting ants.
fun_facts.tiny: Its scales are made of the same stuff as your fingernails.
When it gets scared, it rolls into a tight little ball.
Its long, sticky tongue slurps up ants and ants and more ants!
did_you_know.young: Its long tongue is so big it's tucked away deep inside, all the way down near its tummy.
When it rolls up tight, even a big lion finds its armour very hard to bite through.
It can dig a burrow with its strong claws and curl up to sleep there all day.
Baby pangolins ride along on their mother's tail until they are big enough to walk far.
So many kind people work to protect pangolins so they can keep living safely in the wild.
Pangolins have their own day — World Pangolin Day comes every February to celebrate the only mammal covered in scales.
text.size_comparison.young: It's about as long as your arm, from your shoulder to your fingertips — somewhere around two feet, not counting its long tail.
text.weight_comparison.young: It's quite light — around fifteen pounds, about as heavy as a chubby house cat or a big bag of potatoes.
text.map_narration: Snuffling for ants in warm forests and grasslands, it lives across parts of Asia.
text.sound_description.young: Pangolins are very quiet and gentle, so you mostly hear soft little snuffles and sniffs as they search the ground for ants. When upset, one might let out a low, huffy puff.

sea_otter.name: Sea Otter
sea_otter.habitat: Coastal kelp forests and rocky shorelines

text.summary.young: The sea otter floats on its back like a furry little boat, paddling along with its tummy pointing at the sky. It even cracks open dinner right there on its belly, using a favourite rock as a tool. No animal in the whole world has thicker, softer fur than this one.
text.summary.tiny: The sea otter floats on its back like a tiny furry boat. It opens dinner right on its tummy with a special rock!
fun_facts.young: It floats on its back with its paws tucked up, bobbing along on top of the waves.
When the sea otter wants a snack, it balances a rock on its belly and taps a clam against it until it pops open.
It has the thickest, softest fur of any animal on Earth, with millions of tiny hairs keeping it warm in the cold sea.
Before it falls asleep, it wraps itself in long strands of seaweed so it won't drift away in the night.
Sometimes a whole group holds paws while they sleep, so they all stay together in a cosy little raft.
It tucks its favourite rock into a baggy pocket of skin under its arm to keep it safe for later.
fun_facts.tiny: It floats on its back and bobs on the waves.
It opens a clam by tapping it on a rock on its tummy.
It holds paws with its friends so nobody floats away.
did_you_know.young: Sea otters keep the ocean healthy by eating sea urchins, which lets underwater forests of seaweed grow tall and green.
Their fur is so thick that the cold water never even touches their skin.
They are some of the only animals that use a tool to get their food.
A baby otter is so fluffy that it can't sink, so it floats while its mum dives down to find food.
They eat a huge amount every day to stay warm, munching crabs, clams and sea snails.
Sea otters get a whole week — Sea Otter Awareness Week happens every September to celebrate these clever swimmers.
text.size_comparison.young: Stretched out from nose to tail, it's about four feet long — a little taller than you are, if you lay it down beside you.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs around sixty-six pounds, about the same as a big, friendly dog.
text.map_narration: Floating on its back among the chilly waves, it lives along the rocky coasts of the northern Pacific Ocean.
text.sound_description.young: Sea otters squeak, whistle and chirp to talk to each other, and a baby will cry out with a high little squeal when it wants its mum.

text.summary.young: The axolotl is a smiley little water creature with a frilly pink crown of gills around its head. If it ever loses a leg, a tail, or even part of its heart, it can simply grow a brand new one! Most of its kind live in just one special lake in Mexico.
text.summary.tiny: The axolotl wears a frilly pink crown, and its little mouth always curves up into a smile. If it loses a leg, it can grow a brand new one!
fun_facts.young: Those feathery pink branches around its head are gills, and that's how it breathes underwater.
If it loses a leg, a tail, or even a piece of its heart, it can grow a perfect new one.
It keeps its baby shape and lives in the water its whole life, never crawling onto land.
Its mouth curves up at the corners, so it always looks like it's smiling at you.
An axolotl gobbles up its dinner with a quick, slurpy gulp instead of chewing.
Almost every wild axolotl lives in one special lake near a big city in Mexico.
fun_facts.tiny: Its frilly pink crown helps it breathe underwater.
It can grow a brand new leg if it loses one.
Its little mouth always curves up into a smile.
did_you_know.young: Scientists study axolotls to learn how living things can heal and regrow.
An axolotl can even grow back tiny parts of its own brain.
Most axolotls come in dark colors in the wild, but pale pink ones are easy to spot.
It feels around for food by sniffing and sensing tiny wiggles in the water.
Its name comes from an old Mexican story about a water spirit.
Axolotls are so loved that they have their own special day — February 1st is Axolotl Day, when people celebrate them and help protect their watery home.
text.size_comparison.young: About as long as a banana, or as long as your forearm from your elbow to your fingertips — around ten inches.
text.weight_comparison.young: It's very light — only about as heavy as a small apple, much lighter than one of your shoes.
text.map_narration: Hiding among the water plants, it lives in just one special lake in Mexico.
text.sound_description.young: Axolotls are very quiet and don't really call out, but every now and then one gulps a little bubble of air at the top of the water with a soft pop.

text.summary.young: The clouded leopard is a secretive wild cat with a beautiful coat covered in big, cloud-shaped patches. It's one of the best climbers in the whole cat family, scampering down tree trunks head-first and even hanging upside down from a branch by its back paws. For its size, it has some of the longest teeth of any cat alive today.
text.summary.tiny: The clouded leopard is a shy wild cat with a coat full of cloud-shaped spots. It can hang upside down from a tree branch!
fun_facts.young: Its coat is covered with soft, cloud-shaped patches that help it disappear among the shadows and leaves.
It can climb down a tree trunk head-first, which most other cats simply cannot do.
The clouded leopard can even hang upside down from a branch, gripping with its strong back paws.
Its long tail is almost as long as its body, helping it balance high up in the trees.
It spends much of its life up in the treetops, resting and watching the forest below.
It has very long, sharp teeth for its size, longer than you'd expect on a cat this small.
fun_facts.tiny: Its coat is covered in cloud-shaped spots.
It can climb down a tree head-first.
It can hang upside down from a branch!
did_you_know.young: Its ankles can turn backwards, like a built-in pair of climbing boots, so it can grip the tree as it comes down.
It is so shy and quiet that people almost never see one in the wild.
Its long tail works like a balancing pole when it walks along a high, thin branch.
It can leap from branch to branch and even pounce on a snack while hanging upside down.
Each one's cloudy patches are a little different, like a pattern painted just for it.
Clouded leopards have their own day — August 4 is International Clouded Leopard Day.
text.size_comparison.young: From nose to tail it's a bit longer than you are tall — its body is about three feet long, and its tail adds almost another three feet.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs around forty pounds, about the same as a medium-sized dog.
text.map_narration: High in the leafy treetops, it lives in the warm forests of Southeast Asia.
text.sound_description.young: It purrs, hisses and makes a soft, moaning call to talk to others, but it is usually very quiet so it can stay hidden.

text.summary.young: Even though everyone calls it a bear, the koala isn't a bear at all — it's a pouch animal that carries its tiny baby in a cozy pocket on its tummy. It spends almost the whole day fast asleep in the fork of a eucalyptus tree, snoozing for as long as twenty hours. When it does wake up, it nibbles the leaves of that very same tree.
text.summary.tiny: The koala looks like a soft, sleepy teddy, but it isn't a bear at all. It carries its tiny baby in a warm pocket on its tummy.
fun_facts.young: It can sleep for about twenty hours every single day, all curled up in a tree.
Its baby is called a joey, and it rides in a warm pocket on its mother's tummy.
It eats the leaves of just one kind of tree, called eucalyptus, which smell a bit like cough drops.
A koala has fingerprints so much like ours that they could be mixed up with a person's.
Watch a koala hug a branch and you'll see the sharp little claws that help it climb so well.
Its fluffy ears are big and round, and it twitches them to listen for other koalas calling.
fun_facts.tiny: It can sleep almost all day long, high up in a tree.
Its tiny baby is called a joey and rides in a pocket on its tummy.
It loves to munch the leaves of one special tree.
did_you_know.young: A newborn joey is no bigger than a jellybean, and it climbs straight into the pouch to grow.
Koalas hardly ever need to drink, because they get most of their water from the leaves they eat.
Those eucalyptus leaves are so tough that a koala has to rest all day to turn them into energy.
Each koala has its own private patch of favorite trees that it likes to visit.
A koala's soft, woolly fur keeps it dry in the rain and cool in the hot sun.
Koalas have their own day — May 3 is Wild Koala Day, when people help protect koalas and their gum trees.
text.size_comparison.young: Curled up in a tree, it's about two and a half feet tall — a bit shorter than you, and small enough to hug a branch with its arms and legs.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs about twenty-two pounds, which is around half as much as you, or about as heavy as a big bag of potatoes.
text.map_narration: High in the eucalyptus trees of eastern Australia, it dozes the whole day away.
text.sound_description.young: For such a small, cuddly animal, a koala can make a surprisingly deep, rumbly grunt — a bit like a tiny, snoring pig — when it's calling out to other koalas.

text.summary.young: The wombat is a sturdy, round little digger from Australia, with strong legs and a flat nose perfect for pushing through soil. It scoops out long underground tunnels called burrows, where it stays cool and safe. And here's the silliest secret of all — its poop comes out in the shape of little cubes!
text.summary.tiny: The wombat is a round, sturdy digger that builds cozy tunnels under the ground. And here's a silly secret — its poop comes out in little cube shapes!
fun_facts.young: It digs long underground tunnels, called burrows, with its strong, stubby legs.
Its poop comes out in the shape of little cubes, which it leaves around to say 'this is my home.'
A wombat's pouch faces backward, so dirt doesn't fall in on the baby while it's digging.
Its bottom is covered in tough, thick skin that helps keep it safe down in the burrow.
Watch a wombat trundle along on its short legs — it can suddenly speed up and run surprisingly fast.
It mostly comes out at night, when the air is cool, to munch on grass.
fun_facts.tiny: It digs long, cozy tunnels under the ground.
Its poop comes out in funny little cube shapes!
Its baby pocket faces backward, so dirt stays out while it digs.
did_you_know.young: A wombat's front teeth never stop growing, so they stay sharp from all that munching.
Its burrow can be longer than a school bus, with twisty tunnels and cozy little rooms.
It can leave its cube-shaped poop on top of a rock or log so other wombats can find it.
A wombat is a strong, fast runner over short distances, even though it looks slow and round.
It loves the cool of the night and tucks itself underground to sleep through the warm day.
Wombats have their own day — October 22 is Wombat Day, a day to celebrate these chunky burrowers.
text.size_comparison.young: It's about three feet long from its nose to its tail — close to your own height, but low and round to the ground.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs around sixty pounds, which is more than you, and about as heavy as a big, friendly dog.
text.map_narration: Deep in the cool burrows of Australia, it digs and snoozes the day away.
text.sound_description.young: A wombat is usually quiet, but when it's grumpy or wants another wombat to move along, it makes a low, huffy grunt — a bit like a tiny, cross piggy.

harp_seal.name: Harp Seal
harp_seal.habitat: Arctic sea ice and cold open ocean

text.summary.young: The harp seal is born on the floating sea ice with a coat as fluffy and white as fresh snow. As a baby it can't swim yet, so it waits on the ice while its mother brings it rich milk. Soon its white fur falls away, and it slips into the cold Arctic water to chase fish and tiny sea creatures.
text.summary.tiny: The harp seal is born on the ice with fluffy white fur, just like snow. Soon it slips into the cold water and learns to swim.
fun_facts.young: It is born on the floating sea ice, far out where the ocean freezes over.
A new pup wears a soft white coat that keeps it warm and hides it on the snow.
After a few weeks its white fur falls out, and a sleek silver coat grows in.
Once it learns to swim, the harp seal can dive deep and hold its breath for a long time.
It hunts fish and little wriggly sea creatures down in the dark, cold water.
Grown-ups have a curved dark mark on their backs, shaped a bit like a harp.
fun_facts.tiny: It is born on the ice with fur as white as snow.
Its fluffy white coat keeps it cosy and warm.
When it grows up, it can dive deep under the water.
did_you_know.young: A baby seal drinks such rich, creamy milk that it doubles its weight in only a couple of weeks.
It can close up its nose tightly so no water sneaks in while it dives.
Thick fat under its skin, called blubber, keeps it warm in the freezing sea.
Big dark eyes help it spot fish in the dim light far below the ice.
Whole groups gather on the ice together when it is time for the babies to be born.
Seals have their own day — March 22 is the International Day of the Seal, celebrating seals like the fluffy white harp seal pup.
text.size_comparison.young: It's about five and a half feet long from nose to flippers — a little longer than a tall grown-up is high, if they lay down on the ice.
text.weight_comparison.young: A grown harp seal weighs around two hundred and ninety pounds — about as heavy as seven children your size all piled together.
text.map_narration: Born on the floating ice, it swims through the cold seas near the top of the world.
text.sound_description.young: Harp seals can be surprisingly chatty underwater, making warbles, chirps, and trills, while a hungry pup on the ice cries out with a high little call to its mother.

west_indian_manatee.name: West Indian Manatee
west_indian_manatee.habitat: Warm rivers, estuaries, and shallow coastal seas

text.summary.young: The West Indian manatee is a gentle giant that drifts slowly through warm rivers and along the coast. People sometimes call it a sea cow, because it spends almost the whole day munching on underwater plants. It has a round, whiskery snout that it uses to feel for tasty seagrass.
text.summary.tiny: The West Indian manatee is a gentle giant that floats slowly in warm water. It munches green plants all day long.
fun_facts.young: It drifts so slowly and calmly that it looks like it's floating in a daydream.
Its whiskery snout helps it feel around and find the best plants to eat.
It munches on water plants for many hours every single day.
It comes up to the top to breathe air, then sinks gently back down again.
Its big flat tail pushes it forward with slow, easy strokes.
Long ago, sailors thought these gentle giants were mermaids of the sea!
fun_facts.tiny: It floats slowly and gently, like a daydream.
It munches green water plants all day long.
Its whiskery nose helps it find good things to eat.
did_you_know.young: A manatee can eat a huge pile of plants every day, as much as a tenth of its own weight.
It holds its breath underwater and only needs to come up for air every few minutes.
It has no front teeth at the front of its mouth, just soft lips and bristly whiskers.
Its closest cousin on land is the elephant, even though it lives in the water.
It loves warm water and will swim toward warm springs when the sea turns chilly.
Manatees have their own day — Manatee Appreciation Day comes every March to celebrate these gentle sea cows.
text.size_comparison.young: It's about ten feet long — longer than the tallest grown-up you know lying down, and almost as long as a small car.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs around one thousand two hundred pounds — heavier than a big motorbike, and about as much as thirty children your size all together.
text.map_narration: Drifting slowly through warm rivers and sunny coasts, it munches green plants all day.
text.sound_description.young: Manatees are very quiet, but every now and then they squeak and chirp to one another underwater, especially a mother calling softly to her baby.

text.summary.young: The bonobo is a clever great ape that shares almost all of its body's tiny instructions with people. It lives deep in the warm rainforests of the Congo and is famous for being gentle and kind. When friends start to squabble, bonobos calm things down with hugs and play instead of fighting.
text.summary.tiny: The bonobo is a gentle, clever ape that lives in the warm forest. When friends argue, it makes peace with hugs and play.
fun_facts.young: It shares almost all of its tiny body instructions with people, so it's one of our closest cousins.
When two friends start to squabble, it calms everyone with a hug or a game.
It is so clever that it can use sticks and leaves as little tools.
It swings through the trees and walks on the ground, deep in the rainforest.
It chatters with squeaks, hoots, and peeps to talk with its family.
It spends much of the day high in the treetops, picking ripe fruit to eat.
fun_facts.tiny: It is one of our closest animal cousins.
It swings through the trees with long, strong arms.
It is clever and can use sticks as tools.
did_you_know.young: Bonobos build a fresh, leafy nest high in the trees to sleep in every night.
A clever bonobo can use a stick to fish out tasty bugs or honey.
It only lives in one place in the whole world — the rainforests of the Congo.
Baby bonobos hold tight to their mothers and stay close for many years.
Bonobos remember their friends and love to play games together.
Bonobos have their own day — February 14 is World Bonobo Day, celebrating these gentle, peaceful apes.
text.size_comparison.young: Standing up, it's about four feet tall — a little taller than you are, but shorter than most grown-ups.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs around eighty-five pounds — about as heavy as two children your size added together.
text.map_narration: Deep in the warm rainforests of the Congo, it swings through the trees and makes peace with hugs.
text.sound_description.young: Bonobos are very chatty, using high squeaks, hoots, and peeping calls to talk to their family and let everyone know how they feel.

text.summary.young: The fruit bat has the widest wings of any bat — almost as wide as a grown-up is tall! When the sun goes down, it flaps off into the warm night to find sweet fruit and flowers. It even helps new trees grow by carrying their seeds across the forest.
text.summary.tiny: The fruit bat has the biggest, widest wings of all the bats. It flies out at night to find sweet, juicy fruit.
fun_facts.young: Its wings are really long fingers with soft, stretchy skin between them.
When it sleeps, it hangs upside down and wraps its wings around itself like a cosy blanket.
It has big, dark eyes and can see beautifully in the dark, so it doesn't need to make squeaky sounds to find its way like cave bats do.
At dusk, a fruit bat unfolds its wings and flaps off to find ripe fruit and sweet flower nectar.
Its furry face looks a little like a fox's, which is why some people call it a flying fox.
As it flies from tree to tree, it drops seeds and dusts flowers with pollen — and that helps a whole forest grow.
fun_facts.tiny: It hangs upside down and wraps its wings around itself to sleep.
It flies through the night to find sweet fruit and flowers.
Its face looks a little bit like a fox's face.
did_you_know.young: A fruit bat's wings can stretch wider than a grown-up's arms reach.
It laps up sweet nectar from flowers with a long, soft tongue.
Hundreds of them can hang together in one big tree, all snoozing the day away.
Many of the trees in a rainforest grow from seeds that fruit bats carried there.
It keeps its wings clean and tidy by licking them, just like a cat washing its fur.
Bats have their own day — April 17 is International Bat Appreciation Day, celebrating helpful bats like the fruit bat.
text.size_comparison.young: Its body is only about as long as a banana, but when it opens its wings they stretch almost five feet across — about as wide as you are tall, with your arms reaching out.
text.weight_comparison.young: It's surprisingly light for such big wings — only about two or three pounds, lighter than a full water bottle.
text.map_narration: Flapping out at dusk to find sweet fruit, it lives in the warm forests of Southeast Asia.
text.sound_description.young: Fruit bats squeak, chitter, and squabble when they crowd together in their tree, especially at dusk when everyone is waking up and getting ready to fly.

pallas_cat.name: Pallas's Cat
pallas_cat.habitat: Cold steppe grasslands and rocky slopes

text.summary.young: The Pallas's cat is the fluffiest wild cat in the whole world, with a flat round face whose shape gives it a funny, frowny look! It's only about the size of a pet cat, but its thick, woolly fur makes it look much bigger. It lives in the cold, windy grasslands of Central Asia, where its fur keeps it snug and warm.
text.summary.tiny: The Pallas's cat is the fluffiest wild cat of all, with a flat, round face that looks a little like a frown. Its thick fur keeps it cosy in the cold.
fun_facts.young: Its fur is so thick and woolly that it looks much bigger than it really is.
Its flat, round face shape gives it a funny, frowny-looking expression.
When it wants to hide, it flattens itself low against the ground and freezes as still as a stone.
It lives high up in cold, rocky grasslands where the wind blows hard and the nights are freezing.
It has small, low ears, tucked down on the sides of its head to stay out of the cold wind.
A Pallas's cat creeps quietly through the rocks at dawn and dusk, hunting for little furry creatures to eat.
fun_facts.tiny: It's the fluffiest wild cat in the whole world.
Its round, flat face gives it a frowny-looking expression.
It hides by going flat and still as a stone.
did_you_know.young: The Pallas's cat has more fur for its size than almost any other cat alive.
Its eyes have round pupils, not slits like most other cats.
It can squeeze into cracks in the rocks to keep warm and hide from the wind.
It doesn't run fast, so it sneaks and ambushes instead.
Long ago, people gave it a special name — manul — which is still used today.
Pallas's cats have their own day — April 23 is International Pallas's Cat Day, celebrating this grumpy-looking little wildcat.
text.size_comparison.young: It's about the same length as a pet house cat, around two feet long in the body — but all that fluffy fur makes it look much bigger.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs about nine pounds, around the same as a pet house cat — even though all that fluffy fur makes it look much heavier.
text.map_narration: Hiding among the rocks, it lives in the cold, windy grasslands of Central Asia.
text.sound_description.young: Pallas's cats are usually very quiet, but they can make a strange yelping bark or a little growl, and sometimes a soft purr when they feel calm and safe.

text.summary.young: The cassowary is a huge rainforest bird with a bright blue neck and a tall helmet on top of its head! It can't fly, but it has strong, powerful legs that let it run fast and jump high. It lives deep in the rainforests of New Guinea and northern Australia, where it gobbles up fallen fruit.
text.summary.tiny: The cassowary is a big bird with a bright blue neck and a tall helmet on its head. It can't fly, but it can run very fast.
fun_facts.young: The tall, bony helmet on its head is called a casque, and it crashes through the forest with it leading the way.
It can't fly at all, but its strong legs let it run fast and leap high into the air.
Its neck and head are bright blue, with two soft red flaps that wobble as it walks.
It loves to eat fruit that has fallen to the forest floor, swallowing it whole.
When a cassowary eats fruit and walks away, the seeds it leaves behind grow into brand new trees.
It makes a sound so low and deep that you can almost feel it rumble in your chest.
fun_facts.tiny: It has a tall helmet on the top of its head.
It cannot fly, but it can run super fast.
It gobbles up fruit that falls to the ground.
Its neck is the brightest, shiniest blue.
did_you_know.young: A cassowary can grow as tall as a grown-up, standing up to six feet high.
It is one of the heaviest birds in the whole world.
We always watch this bird from a distance and never chase it, because each foot has a long claw.
It planted many of the rainforest's trees just by eating fruit and wandering off.
Its deep, rumbling call is one of the lowest sounds any bird can make.
Cassowaries have their own day — September 26 is World Cassowary Day, celebrating this big rainforest bird.
text.size_comparison.young: It's a giant of a bird, standing up to six feet tall — as tall as a grown-up.
text.weight_comparison.young: It's very heavy for a bird — about one hundred and thirty pounds, around the same as a grown-up person.
text.map_narration: Booming deep among the trees, it lives in the rainforests of New Guinea and northern Australia.
text.sound_description.young: The cassowary makes a deep, rumbling boom, so low and powerful that you can almost feel it shiver through the air around you.

spectacled_bear.name: Spectacled Bear
spectacled_bear.habitat: Andean cloud forest and high grassland

text.summary.young: The spectacled bear is the only bear that lives in South America, high up in the misty mountains called the Andes. It has pale, creamy rings around its eyes that look just like a pair of glasses, which is how it got its name. The famous storybook bear Paddington comes from Peru — just like this gentle bear, which is the only bear that lives there!
text.summary.tiny: The spectacled bear has pale rings around its eyes that look just like glasses. It is the only bear in all of South America!
fun_facts.young: The creamy markings around its eyes are different on every bear, like a special pattern made just for it.
It's one of the best tree-climbers of all the bears, and it can clamber way up high to find fruit.
It even builds little platforms out of branches to sit on and rest while it eats up in the trees.
Most of its dinner is plants and fruit, and it especially loves the soft middle of a plant called bromeliad.
It lives in cool, cloudy forests so high up that clouds drift right past the trees.
Paddington, the famous storybook bear, comes from Peru — the very same place this real bear calls home.
fun_facts.tiny: It has pale rings around its eyes, like glasses.
It climbs high up into the trees to find fruit.
It loves to eat plants and sweet, juicy fruit.
did_you_know.young: Did you know the pale rings around its eyes are like a fingerprint — no two bears have the same pattern?
It lives higher up the mountains than almost any other bear in the world.
It's a quiet, shy bear that would much rather climb away than meet a person.
It builds cozy nests of bent branches up in the trees to sleep and rest in.
Even though it's a big bear, almost all of its food is plants, berries, and fruit.
Bears have their own day — March 23 is World Bear Day, celebrating bears like the spectacled bear.
text.size_comparison.young: Standing up on its back legs, it's taller than a grown-up — around five or six feet tall — with a big, round, furry body.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs about as much as a small motorbike — close to three hundred pounds — which is heavier than seven children your size all together.
text.map_narration: High in the misty mountains of South America, it climbs through the cloudy forests looking for fruit.
text.sound_description.young: Spectacled bears are usually very quiet, but they make soft grunts, huffs, and gentle purring sounds to chat with each other and with their cubs.

saola.name: Saola
saola.habitat: Wet evergreen mountain forests near streams

text.summary.young: The saola is a gentle, deer-like animal with a smooth brown coat, snowy-white face markings, and two long, straight horns. It lives deep in the misty mountain forests where Laos and Vietnam meet, quietly munching leaves along forest streams. It is so rare and so hard to find that people call it the 'unicorn of Asia' — almost no one has ever seen one!
text.summary.tiny: The saola is a shy animal with a white face and two long horns. It is so rare that people call it the unicorn of Asia.
fun_facts.young: It wasn't discovered by scientists until 1992, which makes it one of the newest big animals we've ever found.
It has two long, straight horns that grow on both boys and girls.
Even though it looks a bit like a deer, its closest cousins are actually cows and buffaloes.
It has big scent glands on its face that it uses to leave smelly messages on leaves and rocks.
It lives only in the misty Annamite Mountains between Laos and Vietnam, and nowhere else on Earth.
It is so shy and secretive that the only wild photos of it come from hidden forest cameras.
fun_facts.tiny: Its two long horns grow on boys and girls.
It looks like a deer, but its cousins are cows.
It lives in misty mountains and nowhere else.
did_you_know.young: It has white stripes and spots on its face that make it look like it's always smiling.
It loves to eat leaves and ferns that grow near forest streams and swamps.
Its horns can grow as long as a grown-up's arm — almost twenty inches!
It is a wonderful swimmer and is happiest in cool, wet, leafy forests.
It is very rare and needs our help, so scientists and helpers work hard to keep its forest safe.
Saola have their own special day — every July 9 is World Saola Day, when people celebrate this rare 'unicorn of Asia' and help keep it safe.
text.size_comparison.young: It grows to about five feet long from nose to tail — a little longer than a young kid is tall, like a real-life unicorn pony tucked away in the forest.
text.weight_comparison.young: It weighs around two hundred pounds, about as much as ten young kids stacked together, or a great big motorcycle.
text.map_narration: Hidden deep in the misty mountains where Laos and Vietnam meet, it lives in cool, leafy forests near quiet streams. It is so shy and so rare that almost no one has ever seen one, which is why people call it the unicorn of Asia.
text.sound_description.young: It is mostly quiet and shy, but every now and then it lets out a soft, gentle bleat, a bit like a baby goat saying hello in the forest.

text.summary.young: The tarsier is a teeny-tiny primate with enormous, round eyes that glow in the dark and fingers that look just like a person's. It lives in the leafy forests of the Philippines, clinging to tree trunks and sleeping all day before waking up at night. Each of its giant eyes is bigger than its brain, which helps it spot bugs in the dark!
text.summary.tiny: The tarsier is a tiny animal with huge round eyes. It lives in trees and hops out at night to find bugs.
fun_facts.young: It has the biggest eyes compared to its body of any animal in the whole world.
Each of its eyes is even heavier than its brain!
It can leap more than ten feet from tree to tree, like a furry little superhero.
It can turn its head almost all the way around to look behind itself, like an owl.
It sleeps all day and wakes up at night to hunt for crunchy bugs.
Its long, springy ankle bones are what give the tarsier its special name.
fun_facts.tiny: Its eyes are huge — bigger than its brain!
It can hop far from tree to tree.
It sleeps all day and wakes up at night.
did_you_know.young: It is only about the size of a grown-up's fist, making it one of the smallest primates on Earth.
It loves to munch on crickets, grasshoppers, spiders, and other little bugs.
It can turn its head super far around to watch for snacks and stay safe.
It clings to tree trunks with its tiny finger pads and zooms between branches.
It is special and needs our help, so scientists and helpers work to keep its forest home safe.
Tarsiers have their own special day — every May 4 is International Tarsier Day, when people celebrate these big-eyed leapers and help protect them.
text.size_comparison.young: Its little body is only about as long as your hand, from your wrist to your fingertips — small enough to curl up in a grown-up's palm.
text.weight_comparison.young: It is super light — only about as heavy as a small apple, or a handful of crayons, so you'd barely feel it sitting on your hand.
text.map_narration: Awake all night with two enormous, glowing eyes, it lives in the warm, leafy forests of the Philippines. It clings to tree trunks and leaps from branch to branch, hunting for tasty bugs in the dark.
text.sound_description.young: It is usually very quiet, but when it wants to chat or feels surprised it makes a high, squeaky peep — and some of its calls are so high that people can't even hear them!

text.summary.young: Gibbons are small apes that live high in the rainforest trees of Southeast Asia. They swing hand-over-hand through the branches so fast it looks like flying, and they can leap across huge gaps between trees. Each morning, gibbon families sing loud, whooping songs together that echo far across the forest.
text.summary.tiny: Gibbons are little apes that swing through the treetops. They sing loud, happy songs in the morning.
fun_facts.young: They are apes, not monkeys — and apes don't have tails!
They swing arm-over-arm through the trees, which is called brachiating, and they can zoom along faster than you can run.
Their arms are super long — longer than their whole body — perfect for reaching the next branch.
They can leap across gaps as wide as a school bus is long without falling.
A mom and dad gibbon sing loud duets together that you can hear from far away.
They have special bendy wrists that let their hands spin around so they never have to slow down while swinging.
fun_facts.tiny: They have super long arms for swinging.
They are apes, so they have no tail at all.
They sing loud songs with their family.
did_you_know.young: They almost never come down to the ground — the treetops are their whole world.
Their loud morning songs help tell other gibbon families, 'This is our part of the forest!'
A gibbon's hands are like hooks, so swinging through the trees is easy and barely tires them out.
Baby gibbons hold tight to their mom's tummy while she swings through the branches.
Gibbons are rare and need our help, so people work hard to protect the rainforests where they live.
Gibbons have their own special day — every October 24 is International Gibbon Day, when people celebrate these singing, swinging apes and help protect them.
text.size_comparison.young: Sitting up, a gibbon is only about as tall as your knees — but stretch its arms out and they reach almost five feet, wider than you are tall!
text.weight_comparison.young: They are very light for an ape — only about fourteen pounds, lighter than a big house cat, which helps them swing without breaking branches.
text.map_narration: They swing through the rainforest treetops of Southeast Asia, in places like Thailand, Malaysia, and Myanmar.
text.sound_description.young: They sing loud, whooping, hooting songs that rise higher and higher, and a mom and dad will sing together in a duet you can hear far across the forest.

numbat.name: Numbat
numbat.habitat: Eucalyptus woodlands and dry forests of Western Australia

text.summary.young: Numbats are small striped marsupials that live in the dry woodlands of Western Australia. Unlike almost every other marsupial, they come out in the daytime to hunt, and they eat one special food: termites. A long, sticky tongue helps them slurp up thousands of tiny bugs every single day.
text.summary.tiny: Numbats are little stripey animals from Australia. They use a long sticky tongue to slurp up termites!
fun_facts.young: They can eat up to 20,000 termites in a single day!
Their sticky tongue is almost half as long as their whole body.
They come out to hunt in the daytime, while most other marsupials sleep.
Bold white stripes run across their reddish-brown backs.
Unlike most marsupials, they don't have a proper pouch for their babies.
They sleep curled up in hollow logs to stay safe and warm.
fun_facts.tiny: They slurp up termites with a long sticky tongue.
They have pretty white stripes on their backs.
They love to play and hunt in the sunshine.
did_you_know.young: They are the only marsupial in Australia that stays awake and busy all through the day.
Their tongue can be about four inches long — almost half the length of their whole body!
They have more teeth than almost any other land mammal, but the teeth are tiny and not for chewing.
They tuck themselves into hollow logs at night and block the opening with their bushy tail.
They are very rare now, but people work hard to protect them and help their numbers grow.
Numbats have their own special day — every first Saturday of November is World Numbat Day, when people celebrate this stripey little marsupial and help protect it.
text.size_comparison.young: From nose to tail they are about as long as a school ruler — around ten inches of body plus a big bushy tail!
text.weight_comparison.young: They are super light — about one pound, even lighter than a guinea pig.
text.map_narration: This little stripey marsupial lives in the dry eucalyptus woodlands of Western Australia.
text.sound_description.young: They are very quiet little animals, but they can make soft clicking and tut-tut sounds when something surprises them.
